newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Chaos and cold beat Siberian workers.
newsitem.headline: Chaos and cold beat Siberian workers.

text.p: Siberian workers, fed up with working without pay for up to six months, staged a mass strike for a third day on Thursday, but their hopes of victory were fading fast.
A local government spokeswoman said about 80,000 miners were on strike, disrupting work at 42 of the region's 76 pits.
But a huge rally scheduled to take place at midday in Kemerovo, capital of the Kuzbass coal-mining region, did not materialise.
Less than 100 people gathered on a snowy square outside local government headqarters and after waiting for 30 minutes in minus 20C (minus 4F) temperatures they started leaving.

"Everyone feels cold," said Nadezhda Udilova, who works at a local chemical plant and who had not been paid since August. "No one from the administration came to talk to us, they simply do not consider us human beings."
Almost 400,000 miners across Russia launched the nationwide strike on Tuesday demanding that the government be replaced and that Moscow pay long overdue wages.
Union leaders say the government owes miners at least 1.5 trillion roubles ($270 million). Consumers owe miners another eight trillion roubles.

Interfax news agency quoted Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin as saying on Thursday the government had allocated 750 billion roubles on December 3 to cover the arrears and would pay 450 billion roubles more in the nearest future.
The miners say they have not seen the money.
The Kemerovo government spokeswoman said that reports that First Deputy Prime Minister Vladimir Potanin would fly to the region for talks with miners could not be confirmed.
"They (government) have decided that the strike is dying out and so they don't need to come," said a disgruntled miner at union headquarters.
Interfax said the number of pits and open-cast mines on strike across Russia grew to 132 on Thursday from 124 on Wednesday.
But in Kemerovo, union leader Viktor Bunin said the problem was the workers were not prepared to push things to the limit.
He said the strike was virtually doomed when only two out of 25 open-cast mines, which produce most of coal in the region, joined it.
"They support us morally but they do not want to ruin their mines and deprive people of heating," he said. "That allows people in power here and in Moscow to continue feeling comfortable."
This sad truth makes many people pessimistic about continuing the strike for any length of time.
"We will soon go back to work," said Zoya Tishanskaya, one of those who had turned up at central Kemerovo square. "They tell us that we are free to leave, and we do not want to lose our jobs."
But others feel more aggressive.
"People in the pits ask my why I cannot do anything," Bunin said. "When I explain things they say: 'We understand, but why don't you go out and find some machine-guns for us.'
"We are getting close to that but I don't want this to happen and I dont think it will, because this would be bad for all of us," he added.
